al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-ix:
The ninth tome of Les Prairies d'Or, printed in 1877, completes Barbier de Meynard's French al-Masudi. The Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi, the Meadows of Gold, is the work of a tenth-century Baghdad scholar who traveled to India, Persia, and East Africa. With this tome the Société Asiatique set stands whole.

Al-Masudi aimed at nothing less than the whole known world. He covers its lands and seas, its ancient kings, and its faiths. The annals of Islam run down to his own time. His method mixes chronicle, geography, and the tales of the road. The French version remains the fullest form of his book in a Western tongue. The long labor of the editors ends here.
australia-felix: Australia Felix is a stirring novel of the early Australian colonies. Its hardy settlers carve out farms and fortunes from the untamed bush. The trials and triumphs of colonial life unfold with color and truth. A rousing and heartfelt pioneer story.
beatrix: Balzac's 1839 novel about a beautiful, heartless coquette and the men she ruins. Set in Brittany and Paris, it is his great study of the femme fatale. Brilliant, bitter, and unforgettable. The Breton coast provides a wild backdrop for this story of ruinous love.

the-danish-history-books-i-ix: Saxo Grammaticus, called Saxo the Learned, wrote his Danish History in Latin in the early years of the thirteenth century, as Douglas B. the-devolutionist-and-the-emancipatrix:
Homer Eon Flint pairs two tales in The Devolutionist and The Emancipatrix. The first opens under the head Out of Their Minds. Mrs. Kinney leads a caller to a locked door with a warning: make no sound, no matter what he sees. She turns the key, and the two step softly into the private study of her husband, Dr. William Kinney.

The room itself is ordinary enough, with book shelves, cases of surgical and psychological instruments, star charts, maps, and astronomical apparatus. Its four chairs are not. Each holds a human being, and none of the four stirs as the pair enters. The doctor sits half reclined, gray head resting wearily on one shoulder. Mrs. Kinney whispers the names: Mr. Smith beside him, and opposite, Mr. and Mrs. Van Emmon, all sunk in complete, motionless sleep.
the-emancipatrix:
Homer Eon Flint's The Emancipatrix opens in a doctor's room, where a blunt question lands: what has come between the geologist Van Emmon and his wife? Van, calm but held tight, traces it to a joint probe of Capellette two months past. Both he and Billie still trust the Venusian formula, he says, and long to visit more worlds by telepathy.

Four friends can project their minds to other planets. What they find there tests their bonds on Earth. Flint, an early pulp hand, blends space travel with close talk of marriage and trust.
the-executor-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magaz:
Mrs. Oliphant's tale The Executor ran in Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume eighty-nine, covering January to June 1861. The volume's title page names William Blackwood and Sons of Edinburgh and their London house in Paternoster Row. The tale opens mid-scene: John Brown declares the woman was certainly mad, a strange speech for the place.

A grim parlour holds two decanters on a bare, shining table, blinds drawn, and half a dozen folk in mourning, their faces a mix of shock and spite. A will has just been read. Oliphant spins greed and duty from that charged room.
the-human-comedy-introductions-and-appen: Balzac's introductions and appendix to the Human Comedy: his famous avant-propos and the plan of the whole vast work. Essential for understanding his design, brilliant and revealing. The architect's blueprint. Balzac's plan is as vast as his achievement.
